name: MTEB: Massive Text Embedding Benchmark
description: MTEB is a massive text embedding benchmark spanning 8 embedding tasks covering a total of 58 datasets and 112 languages. Tasks include bitext mining, classification, clustering, pair classification, reranking, retrieval, semantic textual similarity (STS), and summarization. Through the benchmarking of 33 models on MTEB, it establishes the most comprehensive benchmark of text embeddings to date.
creator: Niklas Muennighoff, Nouamane Tazi, Loïc Magne, Nils Reimers (Hugging Face, cohere.ai)
citeAs: Muennighoff, N., Tazi, N., Magne, L., & Reimers, N. (2023). MTEB: Massive Text Embedding Benchmark. arXiv:2210.07316v3 [cs.CL].
rai:dataCollection: MTEB aggregates existing datasets from multiple sources covering 8 embedding tasks. Some datasets (e.g., ArxivClustering, BiorxivClustering, MedrxivClustering, RedditClusteringP2P, StackExchangeClusteringP2P) were custom-made for MTEB using public APIs from arXiv, bioRxiv/medRxiv, Reddit, and StackExchange. Other datasets were sourced from existing benchmarks such as BEIR, SemEval, and various NLP datasets.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web API, Secondary Data analysis, Web Scraping
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Datasets are sourced from: arXiv public API, bioRxiv/medRxiv API, Reddit posts, StackExchange posts, Amazon customer reviews, Twitter, SemEval datasets (STS11-STS22), BEIR benchmark datasets (ArguAna, ClimateFEVER, CQADupstack, DBPedia, FEVER, FiQA2018, HotpotQA, MSMARCO, NFCorpus, NQ, Quora, SCIDOCS, SciFact, Touche2020, TRECCOVID), Tatoeba multilingual test set, BUCC parallel corpora, and various other NLP datasets.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: For ArxivClustering, multiple categories can be given to a single paper; only the first category is used. For P2P datasets, abstracts are concatenated to the title. For ArxivClustering, three types of splits are created: main category clustering, secondary category clustering within the same main category, and secondary category clustering across all main categories. Subsets of labels are selected and articles sampled to yield splits with varying amounts and sizes of clusters.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Datasets are grouped into three categories based on text length: Sentence to sentence (S2S), Paragraph to paragraph (P2P), and Sentence to paragraph (S2P). For clustering tasks, a mini-batch k-means model with batch size 32 and k equal to the number of different labels is used. For classification, a logistic regression classifier with 100 maximum iterations is trained on train set embeddings. Models evaluate on test splits of all datasets except MSMARCO, where the dev split is used.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations vary by dataset. For clustering datasets (ArxivClustering, BiorxivClustering, MedrxivClustering), cluster labels are generated using categories given to papers by humans. For bitext mining (BUCC, Tatoeba), annotated pairs correspond to translated sentence pairs. For classification datasets, labels were provided by the original dataset creators (e.g., Amazon reviews annotated for counterfactual detection, polarity, sentiment; Banking77 annotated with intents; Emotion dataset with six basic emotions). For STS datasets, labels are continuous similarity scores from 0 to 5. For SummEval, human annotations of machine-generated summaries are used.
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: MTEB is open-source with versioning at dataset and software level to ensure reproducibility. JSON files corresponding to all results are made available together with the MTEB benchmark on the Hugging Face Hub. The benchmark is extensible: new datasets for existing tasks can be added via a single file specifying the task and a Hugging Face dataset name. New tasks require implementing a task interface and evaluator. Community contributions via pull requests are welcomed. A public leaderboard is maintained at https://huggingface.co/spaces/mteb/leaderboard.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Some datasets contain potentially sensitive content, including ToxicConversationsClassification (comments annotated for toxicity), EmotionClassification (Twitter messages with emotion labels), TweetSentimentExtractionClassification (tweets with sentiment labels), and AmazonCounterfactualClassification (customer reviews). The datasets span 112 languages, implicitly capturing geographic and linguistic diversity.
rai:dataSocialImpact: MTEB aims to provide clarity on how text embedding models perform across a variety of tasks, serving as a gateway to finding universal text embeddings applicable to diverse use cases including clustering, search systems, text mining, and feature representations for downstream models. By open-sourcing MTEB alongside a leaderboard, it provides a foundation for pushing the state-of-the-art of available text embeddings and simplifying model selection for both research and industry applications.
rai:dataBiases: MTEB average scores are biased towards tasks with many datasets, notably retrieval, classification, and clustering, due to task imbalance (e.g., summarization consists of only a single dataset). Data contamination is acknowledged as a potential issue: overlap of MTEB datasets with model training datasets is not controlled for in MTEB scores, as the scale of experiments and model pre-training makes this challenging. Multilingual coverage is uneven: retrieval and clustering are English-only, while classification, STS, and bitext mining include multilingual datasets.
rai:dataLimitations: 1. Long document datasets are missing; the longest datasets have a few hundred words. 2. Task imbalance exists, with summarization having only one dataset. 3. Multilinguality is limited: retrieval and clustering are English-only; no code datasets are included. 4. Only natural language modalities are covered; other modalities (e.g., images) are not included. 5. MTEB does not contain datasets such as CodeSearchNet, TyDI QA, XOR QA, or MIRACL.
rai:dataUseCases: MTEB is designed for benchmarking and evaluating text embedding models across 8 tasks: bitext mining, classification, clustering, pair classification, reranking, retrieval, semantic textual similarity (STS), and summarization. It supports evaluation of any embedding model that can produce a vector for each input text. Use cases include training evaluation, testing, and zero-shot evaluation of embedding models. The benchmark is intended for both research and industry applications to aid in selecting the right embedding model.
